stories.title: How Scammers Faked a Video Call With PM Wong
stories.headline_kid: Scammers built a fake video meeting that looked like Singapore's leaders were really on the call — and tricked people out of $5 million.
summary: Imagine joining a video call and seeing your country's leaders talking to you. Sounds real, right? Well, some scammers in Singapore built a fake Zoom call that looked exactly like that. They used old, hard-to-find YouTube videos of Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and other leaders, then cut and stitched the clips together to make it seem like a live meeting was happening.

To make it even more convincing, the scammers added extra 'participants' to the call. These fake people never spoke — their video boxes were just old clips playing on a loop, over and over, so the call looked busy and important. People who joined believed it was a real government event about investing money.

Sadly, this trick worked, and victims lost about $5 million in total. CNA's investigators studied the full footage and worked out exactly how the scammers built the fake call, so they could warn everyone about the tricks used.

This story is a big reminder: just because a video looks real, doesn't mean it is. Scammers are getting cleverer with technology, so it's important to check with trusted sources before believing — or paying for — anything you see online.

lenses.me: If you ever see a video that seems too exciting or important — like a 'famous person' asking for money — stop and tell a trusted adult before doing anything.
lenses.family: Your family should always double-check investment offers through official government or bank websites, never just through a video call link.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates can talk about how videos can be faked, so you're all more careful about what you see online.
lenses.nation: Singapore is working hard to warn people about scams like this, so fewer families lose their hard-earned money.
lenses.world: This shows how fake videos, called 'deepfakes', are becoming a global problem — countries everywhere need to teach people how to spot them.

stories.title: Haze Forces Nearly 600 Schools to Close in Sarawak
stories.headline_kid: The air got so smoky in Sarawak, Malaysia, that almost 600 schools had to shut their doors for two days.
summary: In Sarawak, a state in Malaysia not far from Singapore, the air has turned thick and smoky. This smoky air is called 'haze', and it usually comes from big fires burning far away, with the smoke drifting across the sky.

The haze got so bad — reaching 'very unhealthy' levels — that the government ordered 591 schools across 10 districts to close for two days. That means around 200,000 students suddenly had no school, all because the air outside was too unsafe to breathe.

Areas like Kuching, Sarawak's capital, were badly affected. Doctors and officials worry that breathing in hazy air for too long can hurt people's lungs, especially children and the elderly, so staying indoors becomes important during bad haze days.

Singapore has faced haze warnings before too, especially during the dry season when fires in the region send smoke our way. This news is a reminder for families here to keep an eye on air quality readings, especially if outdoor plans are coming up.

lenses.me: If haze ever drifts to Singapore, your outdoor PE lesson or recess time might move indoors — so always listen to your teacher's instructions.
lenses.family: Your family might want to check the PSI (a number that shows how clean or dirty the air is) before planning outdoor outings this season.
lenses.friends: Friends across the Causeway in Sarawak are missing school right now — it shows how weather can suddenly change daily life.
lenses.nation: Singapore's National Environment Agency watches haze from neighbouring countries closely, so we can be warned early and stay safe.
lenses.world: Haze proves that fires in one country can affect the air that millions of people breathe in other countries too.

stories.title: Singaporean Man Jailed in Malaysia for Insulting a Religion
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean man was jailed and fined after being caught on video making rude remarks about Islam while in Malaysia.
summary: A 56-year-old Singaporean security guard, Mohamed Anim Atam, has been jailed for 14 days and fined RM7,000 (about US$1,733) by a court in Johor Bahru, Malaysia. He had made disrespectful comments about the Quran, the holy book of Islam, while riding in an e-hailing car.

The driver recorded the moment, and the video spread quickly online, going viral. This caught the attention of Malaysian authorities, who charged the man for insulting a religion — something taken very seriously under Malaysian law.

Mohamed Anim pleaded guilty without a lawyer, and the court handed down his punishment on Friday. This case shows that words spoken carelessly, even during a short car ride, can lead to real legal trouble, especially when travelling in another country.

In Singapore too, we have laws that protect racial and religious harmony, because our society is made up of many races and religions living together peacefully. This story is a strong reminder to always be respectful of other people's beliefs, whether at home or abroad.

lenses.me: When you visit another country, remember their rules — especially about respecting religion — can be very strict, even stricter than at home.
lenses.family: If your family travels to Malaysia or anywhere else, it's good to remind everyone to be mindful and polite about local customs and beliefs.
lenses.friends: No matter what religion your classmates follow, it's important to treat their beliefs with respect and never mock them.
lenses.nation: Singapore values racial and religious harmony deeply — this news reminds us why we must always be careful with our words.
lenses.world: Different countries have different laws about what you can and cannot say — something said casually can lead to serious consequences elsewhere.

stories.title: When a Stranger Touched a Child: A Singapore Mall Story
stories.headline_kid: A video of a stranger patting a child's head — followed by a shove — got all of Singapore talking about personal space.
summary: At Roxy Square, a mall in Singapore, something happened that got people talking. A stranger patted a child's head — meant kindly, perhaps — but the child's parent reacted strongly, shoving the stranger away. Someone filmed the whole thing, and the video spread quickly online.

The incident sparked a big discussion. Some people felt the parent was right to protect their child from being touched without permission. Others felt that shoving someone was too extreme a reaction, especially if the stranger meant no harm.

A CNA commentator pointed out something important: children should absolutely know that their bodies belong to them, and it's okay to say 'no' if someone touches them without asking — even a friendly stranger. But she also reminded everyone that responding with violence isn't the lesson we want children to learn either.
This story reminds us that teaching children about personal boundaries matters, but so does teaching them how to speak up calmly and ask for help, instead of reacting with force.

lenses.me: You have every right to say 'please don't touch me' if someone, even a well-meaning stranger, touches you without asking first.
lenses.family: Parents can teach children calm, firm ways to protect their personal space, instead of reacting with force.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can talk about what to do if a stranger makes you feel uncomfortable in public.
lenses.nation: This incident got Singaporeans discussing how we should handle strangers touching children in public places like malls.
lenses.world: This story is a reminder everywhere that respecting personal boundaries, especially for children, truly matters.

stories.title: Woman Dies After Dog Attack at a Pet Hotel in Hong Kong
stories.headline_kid: A worker at a pet boarding centre in Hong Kong sadly passed away after being attacked by a dog she was caring for.
summary: In Hong Kong, a sad accident happened at a pet boarding facility — a place where families can leave their pets to be looked after, like a hotel for dogs and cats. A 33-year-old woman who worked there was attacked by a dog while she was working alone, and she did not survive.
Police are still looking into exactly what happened. It seems the dog she was caring for may have been too big or too unpredictable for one person to handle alone, without help nearby.

This tragic event has made people think carefully about safety rules at pet care businesses. Large or unfamiliar dogs need experienced handling, and workers should never be left completely alone with animals that could be dangerous.

Many Singapore families also use pet boarding services, especially before travelling. This story is a good reminder to check that any pet hotel you use is properly licensed and has enough trained staff to keep both the animals and the workers safe.

lenses.me: If you have a pet, remember that even friendly-looking dogs can act unexpectedly, so always be careful and never approach a dog you don't know without an adult.
lenses.family: Before boarding a family pet during the holidays, it's worth checking that the pet hotel is licensed and has enough staff on duty.
lenses.friends: If a friend's family boards their pet somewhere, you could ask if the place follows good safety practices.
lenses.nation: In Singapore, pet businesses need a licence from AVS (Animal & Veterinary Service) to make sure they follow safety rules — this story shows why those rules matter.
lenses.world: This sad accident is a reminder for pet care businesses everywhere to put the safety of both animals and workers first.
